textbookText: 6. THE FRUIT Fruit is one of the characteristics of flowering plant. After fertilization, the ovule forms seed and ovary developed into fruit. So, fruit is defined as “Matured or ripened ovary, developed after fertilization.” Sometimes, a fruit is formed without fertilization of ovary; this type of fruit is called as parthenocarpic fruit which is seedless (e.g. seedless banana, seedless grapes etc). When only the ovary of the flower develops into the fruit, it is called true fruit (e.g. mango, lichhi etc). In some cases the portions other than ovary, i.e. thalamus or calyx may also take part in the development of the fruit; these types of fruit are called false fruit (e.g. apple, pear etc.)

Parts of fruit Generally, the fruit consists of two parts i.e. pericarp (develop from ovary wall) and seeds (develop from ovules). The pericarp may be dry or fleshy. When pericarp is thick and fleshy, it is differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp. Epicarp is the outer part that forms the skin of fruit. Mesocarp is edible and fleshy part present inner to epicarp. Endocarp is innermost hard region that encloses the seeds.
Figure 2.8.15 Parts of fruit Types of fruit The fruits are basically classified in following three types:
1. Simple fruit A single fruit developing from the ovary of a flower. It may be dry or fleshy. Example: Pea, Mustard, rice, apple, lemon, etc.

2. Aggregate fruit Number of simple fruits or fruitlets develop from an apocarpous pistil of a flower are collected together and form an aggregate fruit. The fruitlets of a group are collectively called etaerio. Example: strawberry, blackberry, Raspberry, custard apple etc.
3. Multiple or Composite fruit The fruit formed by whole inflorescence are called multiple or composite fruits. Examples: pineapple, Jack fruit, mulberry etc.

Functions of fruit a. Fruit protects the seeds from unfavourable conditions. b. The presence of stored food attracts animals that help in dispersal of the seed s. c. The fleshy part of the fruit is responsible for storing the food. d. It provides nutrition to the developing seedling in some cases.

2.8.3 CONCEPT OF TAXONOMY Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms including all plants, animals and microorganisms, based on morphological, behavioural, genetic and biochemical variations. In short, taxonomy is defined as ‘the branch of biology that deals with identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms. Identification is the process of finding the correct name and place of an organism in a system of classification. Nomenclature is the system of giving proper names or scientific names to all the organisms so that these can be easily distinguished from one another. Classification is the Biology, Grade 11 | 158

system of grouping the organisms according to their resemblances or differences in characteristics. Carolus Linnaeus is considered as the father of taxonomy. He is the one who developed a procedure to name and organize species.

Systematics is the science that concerns with identification, nomenclature, description and classification of organisms based on unique properties of every species and groups of species at every level of classification from species to kingdom. It helps to understand the relationship among diverse species. 2.8.4 TAXONOMIC HIERARCHY A taxon (plural: taxa) is a group of organisms that are classified as a unit. It means a category or taxonomic group of any rank like species, genus, family etc. Taxonomic hierarchy or hierarchial system was proposed by Linnaeus. It includes seven categories arranged in descending order from Kingdom to species. The arrangement of taxonomic categories in their proper order on the basis of their taxonomic ranks is called taxonomic hierarchy. There are seven obligate taxonomic categories in taxonomic hierarchy like kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, families, genus and species. These taxonomic categories are further classified as major categories (like- Kingdom, phylum/division, class, order and families) and minor categories (like-genus and species).

Taxonomic Categories a. Species: It is the basic unit of taxonomy. It consist of closely resemble individuals which are genetically distinct, interbreed freely and produce fertile offspring. b. Genus: It is the group of species which have common characters. c. Family: It is the group of one or more genera having common characters. d. Order: It is the group of family with common characters. e. Class: It is the group of order with common characters. f. Phylum/Division: It is the group of class with common characters. The term division is used for plant and the term phylum is used for animals. g. Kingdom: Kingdom is the highest category in taxonomy hierarchy. It is the group of phylum/division having common characters.
